content:
The image shows a split soybean stem cross-section held in hand. Key observations:

- **Affected part**: Stem, split longitudinally to reveal internal tissue
- **Internal discoloration**: The pith and inner cortex show a brownish-gray discoloration running along the length
- **Vascular browning**: Dark brown streaking visible along the vascular tissue/pith area
- **External stem**: Bleached, straw-colored exterior — typical of late-season stem disease
- **No white mycelium** visible inside (rules out White Mold, which has cottony mycelium in the pith)
- **No black sclerotia** visible inside the stem (further rules out White Mold)
- **Pith discoloration is brown/gray**, not completely rotted away

The internal brown discoloration of the pith with an otherwise intact (not hollow/shredded) stem is characteristic of **Brown Stem Rot** (*Cadophora gregata*). Brown stem rot classically shows brown to dark brown internal discoloration of the pith and lower stem when split, often with distinct browning along the vascular tissue, while the external stem may appear relatively normal or slightly bleached.

This is distinct from:
- **Sudden Death Syndrome**: Internal stem tissue remains white/cream; foliar symptoms are primary diagnostic
- **Charcoal Rot**: Shows gray to silver coloring with tiny black sclerotia (microsclerotia) in pith
- **Phytophthora**: Typically shows chocolate-brown discoloration starting near soil line, softer rot
